correlates.management: Manage ruptures conservatively or endovascularly where possible (tissue tears at surgery); keep BP normal; avoid contact sports, isometric exertion and elective surgery; medical-alert bracelet; high-risk obstetric care.

correlates.name: Vasospastic angina
correlates.presentation: 38-year-old woman who smokes and takes sumatriptan for migraines: 3 weeks of crushing chest pain that wakes her near 5 a.m. and lasts 10-15 minutes; she jogs daily without any pain. Her fingers turn white, then blue, in the cold. Normal exam between attacks.
correlates.workup: ECG in an episode: 3 mm ST elevation in II, III, aVF that resolves within minutes of SL nitroglycerin; troponin normal twice; angiography: no fixed narrowing, but IV acetylcholine provokes a reversible focal narrowing of the right coronary.
correlates.management: Calcium channel blocker first line (diltiazem, verapamil or a dihydropyridine); SL nitroglycerin for attacks, long-acting nitrate if needed; stop smoking and triggers (triptans, cocaine, alcohol); avoid beta blockers (unopposed alpha tone).

correlates.name: Vasovagal syncope
correlates.presentation: A 15-year-old girl who skipped breakfast faints while watching her blood being drawn. First she felt warm and nauseated and her vision grayed; she slumped, was out 20 s with a few arm jerks, and was oriented within a minute; no incontinence. Lying: HR 52, BP 86/50, pale, sweaty.
correlates.workup: ECG: sinus rhythm, normal PR and QRS, QTc 410 ms. Glucose 84 mg/dL, hemoglobin normal, pregnancy test negative. Lying and standing vitals 10 min later are normal; heart exam normal.
correlates.management: Reassure; more fluid and salt; at the first warning lie down or sit with legs raised and tense the leg muscles; avoid fasting and known triggers. No further cardiac testing without red flags (exertional, family sudden death, long episode).

correlates.name: Ventricular fibrillation early after MI
correlates.presentation: 58-year-old man 40 minutes into crushing chest pain from an inferior MI, waiting for transfer, suddenly slumps unresponsive with gasping breaths that then stop. No carotid or femoral pulse, BP unrecordable, skin gray.
correlates.workup: Monitor: rapid, chaotic undulations of varying size and shape with no identifiable QRS complexes, P waves or T waves; no pulse. Mechanism: reentry in ischemic, electrically unstable muscle - the most common complication of the first 24 h.
correlates.management: Immediate CPR and unsynchronized defibrillation (biphasic 120-200 J), CPR for 2 min between shocks; epinephrine every 3-5 min; amiodarone or lidocaine if shocks fail; then emergent reperfusion of the culprit artery.

correlates.name: Ventricular free wall rupture
correlates.presentation: 76-year-old woman with hypertension, day 5 after her first MI - a large anterior STEMI never reperfused: brief new chest pain, then sudden collapse. Neck veins distended, heart sounds faint, BP 60 by palpation, then no pulse while the monitor shows an organized rhythm.
correlates.workup: Monitor: organized narrow-complex rhythm with no pulse (PEA); bedside echo: large pericardial collection containing clot, with right atrium and ventricle collapsing in diastole; diastolic pressures equal in all four chambers; no new murmur.
correlates.management: Emergency surgical repair of the myocardial tear; pericardiocentesis only as a bridge; IV fluids; stop anticoagulants. Few survive, so prevention by early reperfusion matters most.

correlates.name: Ventricular septal defect
correlates.presentation: A 6-week-old boy had a silent heart exam in the nursery. Now he takes 40 min per feed, sweats while eating and gains weight slowly. RR 62, HR 160, SpO2 98%; harsh grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur with a thrill at the left lower sternal border; liver 2 cm below the ribs.
correlates.workup: ECG: normal axis, tall R and deep S waves across V2-V4. Chest film: enlarged heart, increased lung markings. Echo: 8-mm opening in the membranous wall between the lower chambers, left-to-right flow, enlarged left atrium and left ventricle.
correlates.management: Small muscular openings usually close on their own - follow with cardiology 1-3 times a year. Large ones with heart failure: diuretics and high-calorie feeds, then surgical patch closure before lung pressures become fixed.

correlates.name: Ventricular septal rupture
correlates.presentation: 69-year-old woman on day 4 after an anterior STEMI from an LAD occlusion: sudden breathlessness and low BP. BP 84/50, HR 118; new loud, harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill; JVP 12 cm, tender enlarged liver, pedal edema.
correlates.workup: Right heart cath: O2 saturation 62% in the right atrium jumping to 84% in the RV and pulmonary artery (left-to-right shunt, Qp:Qs 3:1); color Doppler: jet through a defect in the apical septum; mitral valve competent.
correlates.management: Afterload reduction and inotropes, intra-aortic balloon pump or other mechanical support as a bridge to urgent surgical (or transcatheter) closure of the defect, plus revascularization; outlook is poor without repair.

correlates.name: Viral myocarditis
correlates.presentation: 26-year-old man, 12 days after a week of sore throat and diarrhea: 4 days of chest ache, exertional dyspnea and palpitations. T 38.1 C, HR 116, BP 108/70, an S3 and bibasal crackles. No drug use, no new medications, no recent travel.
correlates.workup: Troponin I 3.1 ng/mL with CRP 120 mg/L (high CRP-to-troponin ratio); ECG: diffuse nonspecific ST-T changes; echo: LVEF 35%, global hypokinesis; normal coronary angiogram. Biopsy: lymphocytic infiltrate beside necrotic myocytes.
correlates.management: Supportive guideline heart-failure therapy (ACE inhibitor, beta blocker, diuretic); no competitive sport for 3-6 months; endomyocardial biopsy only if fulminant or with life-threatening arrhythmia; mechanical support if in shock.

correlates.name: Williams syndrome
correlates.presentation: 3-year-old boy, very chatty and friendly with strangers, with delayed speech and motor milestones and poor feeding as an infant: broad forehead, puffy eyes, full lips, wide mouth. Harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border; irritable, constipated, thirsty.
correlates.workup: Calcium 12.6 mg/dL. Echo: narrowing of the ascending aorta just above the sinotubular junction (gradient 45 mmHg), peripheral pulmonary artery stenoses. Karyotype normal; FISH or microarray: 7q11.23 microdeletion including the elastin gene.
correlates.management: Low-calcium diet and no vitamin D supplements for the hypercalcemia; surgical repair of the supra-aortic narrowing if the gradient is significant; developmental support; test the parents (50% recurrence if one carries it).

correlates.name: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
correlates.presentation: A 24-year-old man with palpitations since his teens was given IV verapamil at urgent care for a fast, irregular rhythm. Within minutes his pulse rose to 260 with wide, varying complexes, BP fell to 84/50 and he nearly fainted.
correlates.workup: Baseline ECG after recovery: PR 0.10 s; a slurred, slow-rising start to a 130-ms QRS that swallows the PR segment; ST-T changes opposite the main QRS deflection.
correlates.management: No AV-nodal blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, beta blockers, adenosine, digoxin); IV procainamide (or amiodarone) if stable, synchronized cardioversion if unstable; cure = catheter ablation of the accessory pathway.

correlates.name: Wolman disease
correlates.presentation: 6-week-old girl with persistent vomiting, watery fatty stools and poor weight gain since 2 weeks of age; abdomen hugely distended by a firm liver and spleen; low-grade fevers; pale; now below her birth weight.
correlates.workup: Abdominal x-ray: both adrenal glands enlarged with dense speckled calcification; AST/ALT mildly high; anemia; lipid-filled vacuoles in lymphocytes and foam cells in marrow; lysosomal acid lipase activity absent in leukocytes.
correlates.management: Enzyme replacement with sebelipase alfa (recombinant lysosomal acid lipase) as early as possible; nutritional support; stem cell transplant in some; untreated, death usually comes within the first year.
